coaching.keys: Count the safeties. One high, throw the seam away from the free safety; two high, hunt the hash.
coaching.vsCoverage: Cover 3 dies on the seams. Quarters wants the back or a scramble.
coaching.commentary: Four receivers running vertical stretches every deep defender at once and asks the quarterback one question.

coaching.keys: Read the flat defender. He widens with the back, throw the stick; he sits on the stick, throw the flat.
coaching.commentary: The most-called play in the system. Two defenders, three receivers, and the quarterback only has to be right about one man.

coaching.keys: Off coverage takes the out. Press takes the slant behind it.
The corner is first if the safety is late. Otherwise it is a hitch-flat triangle on the corner.
coaching.commentary: A bunch makes the rub happen without anybody having to run into anybody.

coaching.keys: Off coverage, take the hitch on rhythm. Press or Cover 0, throw the pressed slot vertical.
Shallow to dig, high-low on the middle linebacker. Against man the shallow keeps running.
coaching.commentary: Two in-breaking routes at two depths on one defender. He is wrong either way.

coaching.keys: Corner first against single high. If the flat defender widens, the shallows sit down.
coaching.vsCoverage: Cover 1, run through the mesh. Cover 3, sit at five or six between the hooks.
coaching.commentary: The whole offense in one play: two shallows rubbing, a corner over the top, a swing to the field.

coaching.keys: Post first, then the mandatory fifteen-yard curl, then the wheel up the sideline.
The Texas route by the back is the hot answer against pressure. Everything else is on rhythm.
Under the outside backer, over the Mike, under the weak safety. The ball comes out on time, off the drop.
Find the window between the corner and the flat defender and sit in it.
High-low the corner on both sides. Pick the softer one before the snap and confirm it after.
coaching.commentary: Mirroring the concept means the quarterback never has a wrong side to look at.

coaching.keys: Count the box. If they are light outside, this is a run call that happens to be a throw.
Sell the fade for one step, then work back inside behind the wall.
coaching.commentary: Against a corner who has been beaten deep twice, this is the third-down answer.

coaching.keys: The stack forces the corner to choose. He takes the post, the wheel runs behind him.
coaching.commentary: A stack means neither defender can jam anybody, so the switch happens clean.

coaching.keys: Against one high safety the inside receiver bends across his face instead of running past him.
Sell the stop for three steps, then climb into the grass between the safeties.
coaching.commentary: The answer to a corner who has been jumping the curl all afternoon.

coaching.keys: The mesh occupies the underneath, and the post runs through where the middle safety used to be.
coaching.commentary: Mesh with a post on top is how the concept attacks three-deep instead of man.

coaching.keys: Four receivers in one band. Throw to whichever window nobody is standing in.
Three levels to the trips side. The corner and the flat defender cannot cover all of it.
The two inside receivers cross deep. In man that is a legal rub fifteen yards downfield.
The receivers clear out vertically and the back sits down underneath the rush.
coaching.commentary: A shovel is a run that starts as a pass, which is why it beats an aggressive front.

coaching.keys: Break to the corner at fourteen and come back across the safety's face at eighteen.
Two in-cuts seven yards apart on the same linebacker.
The shallow runs until somebody carries it. The dig replaces him at eleven.

coaching.install: Isolate the best receiver away from four others and let him win on leverage.
coaching.keys: Everyone else is a decoy who has to be covered anyway.

coaching.commentary: Four receivers to one side against three defenders is arithmetic the defence cannot fix after the snap.

coaching.keys: Three receivers to one side and a tight end alone on the other stretch a single-high safety past what he can cover.

coaching.commentary: The same mesh the defence has practised all week, with the second crosser breaking back the other way.

coaching.keys: The seam route splits the two safeties so neither can help on the corner.
A stacked slot gets a free release. Inside the ten that is all the separation the throw needs.
The vertical clears the hook defender out and the dig runs into the space he left.
Empty with five receivers usually means light boxes. Take the yards on the ground when they hand them to you.
Four vertical routes empty the middle of the field, then the ball goes there.

coaching.commentary: Throw Stick four times. The fifth one the linebacker jumps and the seam is behind him.

coaching.keys: If the corner has started squatting on the tunnel, the post behind it is the whole reason to keep calling it.
The short post holds the safety and the deep post runs past him. Seven blockers means the quarterback gets to wait.

coaching.install: Five receivers spread evenly across the width, all at five to eight yards. Throw to whichever one is uncovered.
coaching.keys: The ball comes out on the third step every time.

coaching.install: Down, down, back. The fullback kicks the end, the backside guard wraps to the playside backer.
coaching.commentary: If the end squeezes, the fullback logs him and the back bounces.

coaching.install: Guard kicks, tackle wraps. The back's first step goes away from the play and sells it.
coaching.commentary: Counter punishes a defense that has learned to chase Power.

coaching.install: The modern spread version: guard and H-back pull instead of guard and tackle.
Let the three-technique come. The backside guard traps him and the back runs off his tail.
coaching.commentary: A penetrating tackle is a gift to a trap team.

coaching.install: The fullback isolates the linebacker in the hole. The back reads that one block and goes.

coaching.keys: Get the ball outside before the edge sets. If the corner squats, crack him and run past.

coaching.install: Both guards pull. The wingback takes it wide behind them.
coaching.commentary: The play the rest of the Buck series exists to set up.

coaching.install: Two double teams, nobody pulls. The back reads the linebacker off the second level.
coaching.commentary: Power's angles without Power's timing risk.

coaching.install: The H-back crosses the formation and whams the three-technique nobody blocked.
The backside tackle pulls and leads through the hole. Cheaper than Power out of an empty backfield.
Down block everything inside, pull the playside guard around the kickout.

coaching.keys: The motion has to be full speed at the snap or the timing is gone.
coaching.commentary: Even when it gains three yards it moves the defense sideways, which is what the rest of the run game wants.

coaching.keys: Read the end man on the line. He chases the sweep, the quarterback keeps it inside behind the pull.
coaching.commentary: The back and the quarterback swap the give and keep roles compared to a normal zone read.

coaching.install: Back away, quarterback downhill behind the counter blocks.
coaching.keys: Read the backside end. If he chases the sweep the quarterback has a gap with two pullers in it.

coaching.install: Covered linemen pin down, uncovered linemen pull around. Nasty splits shorten the run to the edge.
The guard folds around the centre's down block. A different angle on the same gap.

coaching.keys: Power action pulls the linebackers, and the quarterback comes out the back door.
The receivers crack inside and the pullers take the corner. Numbers on the edge decide it.
Show them a drop, then run at the rush lanes they just vacated.
coaching.commentary: Best called on a down where the defence has already decided you are throwing.

coaching.keys: Running the quarterback puts an extra blocker on the play. On the two-yard line that is the whole argument.
Full-speed jet motion one way, counter the other. The front cannot honour both.

coaching.install: Three tight ends, one wham block, one gap. Nothing clever about it.
Everybody is inside the tackle box, so every block is a short one and every defender has to be right.
coaching.commentary: The whole formation is a short-yardage answer that also happens to run all day on first down.

coaching.keys: Same first step as Power, opposite hole. The linebackers have to be honest for one count.
The extra lineman to the strong side gives you one more gap than the defence has aligned to cover.
coaching.commentary: Make them check their alignment while the play clock runs.

coaching.keys: Three receivers away pull the defence out of the box and the run goes to the tight end side.
Two pullers arriving from the backside while the back's first step goes the other way.

coaching.commentary: One blocker and one linebacker in a phone booth. Everything about the play is that collision.

coaching.keys: Three tight ends on the field usually buys a heavy box. Get outside it.
Let the three-technique come upfield, then trap him from the other side with the tight end.
The back runs one way, the quarterback follows two pullers the other way, and the end decides.
The quarterback attacks the edge and the shovel goes underneath him into the vacated gap.

coaching.commentary: Run Power eighteen times and this is what the strong safety's eyes give you on the nineteenth.

coaching.keys: Counter action pulls the secondary one way. The throw goes back to where they started.
Sell the sweep hard. The reverse only gains what the first fake earns.
Everyone squeezes inside-out and drives as one surface. The back finds the crease after contact.

coaching.install: Covered, block him. Uncovered, combo with your neighbour and climb.
coaching.keys: Aiming point is the playside A gap. Press it, then take what the first down lineman gives you.
coaching.commentary: The most-run play in football because it is right against every front without being checked.

coaching.keys: Press the edge until the defense runs with you. The cutback opens up behind their pursuit.

coaching.install: The H-back crosses the formation to kick the backside end, which is the one defender zone rules cannot account for.

coaching.keys: The landmark sits between inside and outside. The back runs a track and takes what the first down lineman gives him.
Leave the backside end unblocked and read him. He crashes, pull it; he sits, give it.
coaching.commentary: Blocking one fewer defender is how a spread offense gets even numbers without an extra tight end.

coaching.install: Covered linemen pin down, uncovered linemen pull around. A zone play with gap-scheme angles.

coaching.keys: Zone blocking with counter backfield action. It is the answer to a fast-flowing linebacker.
Three levels to the boot side. Take the first one that is open and get the ball out.
coaching.commentary: The play the wide zone game is really running toward.

coaching.install: Zone rules on a fullback dive. The option game's answer to a defense that stops the triple.

coaching.keys: The back runs the sweep track and the quarterback keeps it downhill. Roles inverted from a zone read.
The tight end fakes the slice and arcs to the alley instead, which is the read key's tell.
The pistol depth lets the back get downhill on the same track a shotgun back has to drift for.

coaching.install: Every lineman is on a double team. The back finds the crease off the second level.
The H-back slices back across to take the end that zone rules cannot reach.

coaching.keys: Crack the overhang and let the tight end arc to the corner.
The H-back arcs past the read key to the alley player, so a keep has a lead blocker.
Under centre the back is already downhill; the fullback takes the first linebacker to show.
Full wide-zone action. If the safety takes one step downhill the post is behind him.
Getting the ball outside before the front can run with it is the whole play.
No dive phase. Attack the edge and make the outside backer wrong.
Two extra blockers on the edges mean the zone can stay tight to the box.
Press the edge and read the reach block. The cutback is always there if the front over-runs.
Trips to the field takes two defenders with it. Run at the tight end into the lighter side.

coaching.install: The first run install of most seasons. Aiming point is the playside A gap with the read on the first down lineman.

coaching.keys: The H arcs past the read man to the alley player, so a pull has a blocker in front of it.
The fullback crosses the formation to kick the backside end, which is what makes the cutback legal.
Two tight ends combo to the linebacker. The back presses the outside hip and cuts off the double team.
The back sweeps away from the line's flow and the quarterback keeps it inside if the end chases.
Motion at full speed at the snap. The whole play is the runner beating the edge defender to the corner.
Four vertical routes clear the box. Let the rush come upfield and run underneath it.
Anyone covered blocks down, anyone uncovered pulls. The rule sorts itself out against any front.
No protection at all on the backside, so the ball is out on the fifth step regardless of what is open.
Full zone footwork, then throw into the window the filling linebacker just left.
Both receivers crack inside and the toss gets outside of them before the corner can replace.

coaching.commentary: Most defences check their alignment to an unbalanced set. Snap it before they finish.

coaching.keys: The slice block and the read key are on the same side, so the quarterback reads the next man out.
Deep, intermediate, and flat on one side. Whoever the corner and the flat defender cannot both cover is open.
coaching.commentary: Three receivers at three depths against two defenders. One of them comes open every time.

coaching.keys: Two in-breaking routes at different depths. Read the underneath defender's depth and throw off him.
Three receivers in one horizontal band. Throw to the open grass between them.
High-low the corner. If he sinks, throw the hitch; if he squats, throw over him.
The oldest two-man game in the book. The flat defender cannot have both.
The seam clears the safety out of the dig's window. The dig is the throw.
Shallow underneath, basic cross behind it. Against man the shallow wins on the rub.
Same read as the Air Raid version, run out of a pro personnel group.
Fastest answer to pressure in the book. Ball is out on the third step.
Five eligibles, no protection help. The ball has to come out on time or not at all.
Six-yard mesh out of pro personnel. Sit against zone, keep running against man.
Sell the run with the line and the back. The post is only there if the safety bites.
coaching.commentary: Play action works on first and second down, when the defense still has to respect the run.

coaching.keys: Invite the rush, let it go by, and put the ball behind it. Patience is the whole play.
Shallow first against man, dig first against zone. Same play, two answers.
Everything flows right and the quarterback comes out left alone. Take the flat, then the crosser.
coaching.commentary: It only works if the run game has earned the linebackers' attention.

coaching.keys: Two crossers at two depths going opposite ways. Condensed splits give them room to run.
A triangle on the flat defender: corner over the top, spot underneath, flat outside.
Stem at the post hard enough to turn the corner's hips, then break back outside.
Sell the stick, then climb. A linebacker who has been driving on the stick all game is beaten.
coaching.commentary: The complement to Stick, and it only exists because Stick gets called so often.

coaching.keys: Hitches outside, seams inside. Against pressure it is the fastest answer that still gains ten.
The over route works against the grain at seventeen. Nobody runs with it in zone.
Nasty splits give the fade room to work. Throw it where only he can reach it.
The back sells outside then cuts under. A linebacker covering him in space loses every time.
The slot works back inside behind two blockers while the outside clears.
Full run fake, then move the pocket away from the pressure and read the flat defender.
Two crossers at different depths off run action. Man coverage has to run through traffic to stay with them.
The tight end breaks away from leverage at eight yards and the quarterback throws off the same picture.
Three-step drop, ball out on time. The flat route and the slant put the same defender in a bind.
Sell the flat, then break back inside. A linebacker in man coverage cannot change direction with a back.
Three routes at three depths on one side. The flat defender picks one and the quarterback takes another.
Motion changes the count on the perimeter after the defence has already declared.

coaching.commentary: Two backs stay in and block, which buys the extra beat a twenty-yard post needs.

coaching.keys: Show protection for a beat, then release into the space the linebackers vacated.
Two out-breaking routes on the same corner at eight and fourteen.
Two blockers in front of one slot receiver in space is a good trade on any down.
A three-man triangle out of a bunch, with the fade backside if they load the bunch.
The inside post occupies the free safety and the outside post runs past where he was.
Empty means no protection help, so the ball has to come out. Two of the five routes finish out of bounds.
Count the box before the snap. Six defenders on six blockers means hand it off; seven means throw it.
coaching.commentary: The entry-level RPO, and still the one that gets the most yards for the least risk.

coaching.keys: Read the overhang or the down safety. If he fills, the glance is behind him over the linebacker's head.
Punishes a linebacker who triggers downhill on run action. The window is exactly where he left.
Stretch action holds the edge. If the flat defender chases the run, the stick is uncovered.
Gap-scheme action pulls the linebackers hard. The tight end pops into the space they left.
Gap scheme with a perimeter answer. Same pre-snap count, harder run behind it.
Two reads on one snap: the corner's cushion before the ball moves, the end after it.
coaching.commentary: A genuine three-way option out of the gun, and the whole point of storing two reads on one play.

coaching.keys: The read is inverted: it looks like a pass first and the run is the alternative.
Horizontal stress before the snap and vertical stress after it.
Five verticals clear the box out. Everything after that is one man to beat.
If the corner is more than seven yards off, take the free five.
Run call with a downfield peek. If the middle of the field opens, take it; otherwise hand it off.
The tight end pops into the window the linebacker leaves when he fills the A gap.
Four to one side. Count them; if they do not match it you never have to hand it off.
Split-zone action holds the backside. The glance runs behind the safety who filled.
The run goes one way; if the backside overhang chases it, throw behind him.
Gap-scheme run action moves the second level further than zone does, so the window is bigger.
A two-man triangle on the flat defender, attached to a run. He is wrong three ways.
Empty says pass. Two pullers say otherwise.
coaching.commentary: Nobody has a spy on the quarterback out of an empty set on third and two.

coaching.keys: Jet motion moves the whole second level sideways. The glance runs into what they left.
Run to the tight end, throw to the trips. The safety cannot be in both places.
Count the defenders over the four receivers. Three means throw it.
A pulling guard moves the second level further than any zone step does.
Both answers attack the edge, so the defence has to defend the same grass twice.
Read the middle linebacker's depth. If he drops, hand it off.
The arrow puts a body in the flat immediately, so the overhang has to choose before the mesh finishes.
A stacked receiver cannot be pressed, so the slant is on time every snap.
The shovel is the run. The fade is what you take when the edge crashes to stop it.

coaching.commentary: The oldest short-yardage math there is: add the quarterback to the run game and the box is even again.

coaching.keys: Full zone mesh with two crossers behind it. If the linebackers step up, throw over them.
Snap it before the defence is set. The play is easy; the speed of getting to the line is the point.
Four vertical routes against a defence that has not had time to substitute.
The run goes to the single-receiver side and the throw goes to the three-receiver side.

coaching.commentary: Triple option out of a pistol set, which puts the same read on the defence from a modern look.

coaching.keys: The back is in space with two blockers before the rush has covered five yards.
One call, run and pass attached, snapped fast enough that the call never gets checked.

coaching.install: Read the first man outside the playside tackle for the give. Read the next one for the pitch.
coaching.commentary: Two defenders blocked with two decisions instead of two blockers. That is the whole offense.

coaching.install: The read moves inside to the playside tackle. Answer to a defense widening for the veer.
One read, no pitch. Simpler when the pitch key is unreadable.
The dive track moves outside the tackle and the slot loads the support defender.

coaching.keys: Pre-snap motion, immediate pitch. The fastest way a flexbone gets to the edge.
coaching.commentary: It exists so the defense cannot sit inside waiting for the veer.

coaching.install: Veer action one way, option the other. Punishes a defense that has started to flow.
Answer to a tackle who has learned to crash the dive.
The fullback carries out the dive fake and the quarterback follows him into the same gap.

coaching.keys: Two throws all game, and this is one of them. The safeties have been in the run fit for three quarters.

coaching.install: Straight pitch to the slot without motion. Slower than Rocket, better angles.

coaching.commentary: Once a game, off the look that has already gained forty yards on the ground.
Three fakes before the ball ever goes anywhere. It works because the first two are real plays.

coaching.install: One read instead of two. The quarterback attacks the outside shoulder of the pitch key immediately.
coaching.keys: Pitch relationship is four yards behind and four wide. Keep it the whole way.
When a team is fast-flowing the pitch key, block him and run downhill off his tail.

coaching.install: The same read as Inside Veer with a tight end and a third back instead of two split ends.
coaching.commentary: Bring this out when the game is a possession game and the sideline wants the clock to keep moving.

coaching.keys: Fullback belly action first, then the quarterback presses off the kickout.
The corner has squatted on Rocket for two quarters. This is the throw over the top of him.

coaching.install: Full dive fake, then throw behind the linebackers who filled it.
coaching.keys: Against a team that walks both safeties down, this is the softest yardage on the call sheet.
Triple option with a throw attached backside, so a fast-flowing linebacker costs them yards.
Read the first defender inside, and put a blocker in front of the keep.
Full-speed motion means the pitch man is already at the edge when the quarterback gets there.
The same triple read from a pistol depth, which gives the dive back a downhill start.
Dive fake to the strength, then option the other way against a defence that has already flowed.
Motion one way, run the other, and still have a pitch phase on the back end.

coaching.commentary: Three backs and two tight ends on fourth and one. Everyone in the stadium knows and it works anyway.

coaching.keys: Trap the tackle who has been squeezing the dive and keep the pitch phase behind it.

coaching.commentary: Two throws a game, and the safeties have been in the run fit since the opening drive.

coaching.keys: The linebackers step up on the dive every single snap. This is the ball over their heads.
When the corners start crashing on the pitch, throw it out there before they arrive.
Show the option pitch phase, then run straight through where the linebackers were standing.
Motion out and back so the defence has to re-declare its edge twice before the snap.
Inside the five the read shortens to one man and the give is usually right.
The receiver cracks the force player and the pitch gets outside of it.
No read at all. Straight downhill with a lead blocker, which keeps the dive honest for the option.
Move the launch point. An option quarterback throwing on the run is a harder problem than one in a pocket.
Three ways to get the ball to three different players on the same snap, all inside twelve yards.

coaching.install: Both guards pull. The wingback takes it wide behind them and the fullback fakes the trap.
coaching.commentary: Everything else in the Buck series is a lie told about this play.

coaching.install: Identical backfield action to the sweep. The fullback keeps it and runs through the trap.

coaching.keys: Three levels away from the sweep flow. The linebackers have already left.
coaching.commentary: The third play of the series, and the one that scores.

coaching.install: Down blocks inside with the wing sealing the edge.
Fullback downhill off the belly fake. The complement to Down.

coaching.keys: Belly fake, then a post-corner combination on a safety who is already downhill.
Full speed at the snap. The motion is the play.

coaching.install: Jet motion pulls the front sideways, the fullback traps back against it.

coaching.commentary: Only works after Buck Sweep has gained ground twice.

coaching.install: The tackle pulls and traps, which nobody scouts for.

coaching.keys: Half the field, three levels, and the quarterback can always run it.
The wing blocks down and the fullback kicks. Everything inside is angles.

coaching.install: No pulls and no fakes. This one beats the defence to the edge with pure width.

coaching.commentary: The safety has come downhill on Buck Sweep all night. He gets one chance to be right.

coaching.keys: Run Jet Sweep four times first. Save this one until the backside corner starts chasing.

coaching.install: Everyone squeezes to the ball and drives as one surface. The back follows the pile.

coaching.keys: Sweep flow takes the second level with it. The screen goes where they left.
Three receivers on one side at three depths. The flat defender covers one of them.
Two pullers and two wings mean four blockers arrive at the edge before the defence can widen.
The tackle chasing the sweep gets trapped from the inside on the very next snap.

coaching.commentary: The third play of the series, and the one that scores after the first two have done their work.

coaching.keys: Identical backfield action to Buck Sweep with the ball going back inside.
The linebackers have filled the trap all game. The corner route replaces where they were.
Belly fake to the fullback, then attack the edge with a pitch phase behind it.
The motion man traps the tackle who has started chasing jet sweep.
An extra lineman on the sweep side means one more blocker than the defence has aligned to handle.
Run away from the wing after two quarters of running toward him.

coaching.commentary: Everyone chases the waggle. The throw goes back to the field they left.

coaching.keys: The eligible player has to report to the official before the snap, and nobody covers him the first time.
Full-speed motion moves the second level sideways. Throw behind it.
Down blocks inside and an option phase outside, which is Wing-T geometry with a modern read on the end.
The quarterback runs at the edge and flips it back underneath to the wing.
Same power rules with an I backfield, so the tailback gets downhill with speed.

coaching.commentary: Once a season, and only after the criss cross run has already scored.

coaching.keys: One step to the sweep side, then straight back into the gap the flow vacated.
Belly action to the strength and a three-level flood away from it.
Find the soft spot and sit. Do not drift — the quarterback is throwing to where you stopped.
Ball out on the second step. This is the answer when the rusher is getting home.
coaching.commentary: The single most useful play in a beginner flag playbook.

coaching.keys: The over runner goes first. Settle that in practice so nobody hesitates at the mesh point.
coaching.commentary: In a thirty-yard width two crossers are almost impossible to cover in man.

coaching.keys: One defender, two receivers, two depths. Throw to whichever one he is not covering.
Three verticals against three deep defenders is a footrace, and it takes the whole clock.
coaching.commentary: Only call it with time on the play clock and a quarterback who can get it there.

coaching.keys: Deep, intermediate, shallow, all to one side. Take the open one and get out of bounds.
A stack means nobody can press. The two receivers split one defender vertically.
The two crossers create a natural rub. Order matters: the deeper one clears first.
Sell the corner hard. The safety has to commit before the post breaks back.
Three receivers in a triangle. Against man somebody gets picked without anybody committing one.
The centre is eligible the instant he snaps it. Nobody covers him until you have run this once.
coaching.commentary: Free yards in most youth leagues, and it stays free longer than it should.
Run the hitch three times first. The fourth one is a touchdown.

coaching.keys: The quarterback cannot run it, so the exchange has to be clean and it has to be behind the line.
coaching.commentary: Illegal inside either no-run zone, so check where the ball is spotted before you call it.

coaching.keys: The receiver reads leverage and breaks away from it. Quarterback and receiver have to see the same thing.
A defender who has covered a back all game does not expect him to run vertical.
Inside the five you have to throw it anyway. Put it where only your receiver can get it.
coaching.commentary: The no-run zone makes the goal line a passing situation by rule, so have three of these.

coaching.install: Three receivers surround one defender at three depths. Throw to whichever one he leaves.
coaching.keys: The spot sits down in front of him. The flat runs under him. The corner goes over him.
Two in-breaking routes five yards apart. The middle defender can only carry one of them.
The stacked pair crosses at three yards. Whoever is chasing has to run through the other one.
coaching.commentary: The wheel is the throw. The post is there to take the safety out of the picture.

coaching.keys: The vertical route pulls the middle defender up. The dig replaces him at eleven yards.
The shallow keeps running until somebody stops it. Against man that is usually nobody.
Both routes finish out of bounds. With the clock running that is the whole point of the call.
The two deep routes cross at twelve yards. Man defenders run into each other there.
The outside receiver clears flat and shallow. The inside receiver comes off his hip.
coaching.commentary: Check your league rules on contact. A legal rub in flag is a route that gets in the way on its own.

coaching.keys: Sell the inside break hard enough that the defender plants, then come back outside.

coaching.commentary: Throw the six-yard out twice. The third time the corner jumps it and this is behind him.

coaching.keys: Ball out before the rusher arrives. Everything after the catch is the back against one defender in space.
Move the quarterback toward the routes. The rusher has further to travel every step.

coaching.install: Three vertical routes and the snapper underneath as the outlet.
coaching.keys: With a seven-second clock this is the deepest call in the book. It needs a clean snap and a decision.
Both outside routes break out and take the coverage with them. The snapper walks up the middle.
The exchange happens behind the line and the quarterback stays put. Two yards is a good outcome here.
coaching.commentary: Illegal inside either no-run zone, so check the spot before you send it in.

coaching.keys: Motion sets the defence running one way and the handoff goes the other.
The handoff has to be behind the line and the second passer has to stay behind it too.
coaching.commentary: One of these a game. The safety who has bitten on the sweep twice is the target.

coaching.keys: The receiver stops at eight and comes back for it. A defender running to the corner cannot stop with him.
Two routes on one defender at two depths. He declares and you throw the other one.
The front man of the stack slants first and takes the coverage with him.
The corner route breaks at nine and finishes at the pylon. Throw it where he is going.
Two receivers cross underneath and the third runs the fade off the traffic they leave.
First read, first step. Inside the five this is the fastest ball in the book.
Every route finishes out of bounds. Catch it and get your feet outside.
Thirteen yards, snap the head back to the sideline. Against a corner who is bailing it is uncoverable.

coaching.commentary: One throw, one chance. Take it while there is still time for another snap after it.

coaching.keys: Catch it, turn, and get out. Seven yards and a stopped clock is a good outcome.

coaching.install: Against two rushers every route shortens by three yards. This is the version of the play that assumes they are coming.

coaching.keys: Let them come, then throw behind them. Two rushers who miss are two defenders out of the play.
One deep route, one wheel, one outlet. If the deep ball is not there the checkdown always is.
The crosser starts inside and finishes at twelve on the far hash. It takes time, so it needs a clean pocket.

coaching.install: The same mesh, with both crossers settling in the first open grass instead of running through.
coaching.keys: Against zone they sit down in the first window. Against man they keep running. The receivers decide.
Isolate your best route runner and let him break off whatever the defender gives him.
coaching.commentary: It only works if the quarterback and the receiver watch the same defender.

coaching.keys: Two crossers on the same track. The trailing defender has to fight through the first one.
The outside receiver slants in and the inside receiver breaks out behind him.
The post occupies the deep middle defender and the dig runs underneath him.
A linebacker who has covered this back all game is not running with him up the sideline.

coaching.commentary: Run Stick twice. The third time the hook defender jumps it and the seam is wide open.

coaching.keys: Motion tells you man or zone before the snap. If a defender travels with him, throw it away from the traffic.
Motion the flat route across so the defence has to re-fit while the ball is coming out.
The first throw goes backwards, which keeps it a legal forward pass for the second one.
coaching.commentary: Everybody on that sideline turns to watch the first catch. That is the whole play.

coaching.keys: Three receivers to one side and the snapper leaking out the back door on the other.
Show the drop, let the rusher run past, then hand it off behind him.
coaching.commentary: Illegal inside either no-run zone, so check the spot first.

coaching.keys: Two exchanges, both behind the line. Run the jet sweep first so they chase it.
coaching.commentary: Illegal inside either no-run zone.

coaching.install: Three deep, four under. The extra man in the box shows up in the run fit, which is the whole reason to play it.
coaching.keys: Corners bail to the deep third at the snap. The curl-flat defenders expand with number two.
coaching.commentary: Vulnerable to four verticals on the seams and to a well-timed flood.

coaching.keys: Man across the board with a free safety in the deep middle and a rat in the hole.
coaching.commentary: Loses to a mesh and to any crossing concept that generates a legal rub.

coaching.keys: Corners squat and re-route number one. Safeties split the field in half.
coaching.commentary: The seam and the deep middle hole are where it dies, which is what Tampa 2 exists to fix.

coaching.keys: The Mike runs the deep middle to about twenty and takes the seam away.
coaching.commentary: Costs you a run defender in the box to buy the middle of the field.

coaching.keys: Played as a pattern match. Safeties become run defenders the moment number two goes flat.
coaching.commentary: Nine in the box against a run and two-high against a pass, if the safeties read it right.

coaching.keys: Five defensive backs against eleven personnel. The nickel plays the curl-flat to the field.
The base call against a spread offense on early downs.
Trail technique underneath with two-deep help over the top.
coaching.commentary: The safest man call, and the one that gives up the most underneath.

coaching.keys: Quarters to the field, Cover 2 to the boundary. Four plus two is six.
coaching.commentary: A hash-dependent call. It stops being clever when the ball is in the middle of the field.

coaching.install: Three down linemen two-gapping so four linebackers can play free.
Stacked linebackers make the front unreadable before the snap.
coaching.commentary: The whole point is that the offense cannot count the box until the ball moves.

coaching.install: Six on the line, everybody in a gap, man behind it.
coaching.commentary: One play-action away from a walk-in touchdown, which is the trade you accept on the two-yard line.

coaching.keys: Five rush, three under, three deep. The end drops into the vacated curl.
coaching.commentary: Pressure without gambling the deep part of the field.

coaching.keys: Both linebackers walk up into the A gaps. Whether they come is decided after the centre declares.
coaching.commentary: Half the value is that the offense has to slide protection before it knows anything.

coaching.keys: The nickel comes off the slot's outside shoulder, which nobody in the protection is assigned to.
Two-high shell before the snap, one-high after it, and the strong safety arrives late.
Everybody not covering somebody is coming. There is no help anywhere.
coaching.commentary: A hot route or a slant beats it every time, so call it when the offense has no time to find one.

coaching.keys: Three deep, everyone else underneath. The base call in most passing leagues.
Two halves over the top. Corners take the flat and re-route the outside receiver.

coaching.commentary: With no rush, man coverage in 7v7 is a test of how long a defender can run.

coaching.keys: One rusher from seven yards, three underneath, one deep.
coaching.commentary: The safest call in flag, and the reason curls and sticks exist.

coaching.keys: Everyone has a man, one safety helps deep. Watch the crossers.
coaching.commentary: Mesh and Quick Cross are designed specifically to beat this.

coaching.keys: Two rushers, everyone else in man with no safety.
coaching.commentary: Quick slants beat it. Call it when the offense has to go deep anyway.

coaching.keys: Nobody rushes. Five defenders cover three receivers and wait for the seven-second clock.
coaching.commentary: The clock is the pass rush. Against a quarterback who holds it, this is a sack every time.

coaching.install: The line shifts away from the tight end and the Sam walks up on him. Every gap is accounted for without a safety in the box.
coaching.keys: Sam sets the edge to the tight end. Will is free to run to the ball.
Sam takes the tight end from a head-up alignment. Everyone else plays man with a free safety over the top.
coaching.commentary: The best call in the book against a heavy set that wants to throw to the tight end.

coaching.install: Quarters rules until number two breaks to the flat. Then the corner comes off number one and traps him.
coaching.keys: The safety takes number one vertical the moment the corner triggers.
coaching.commentary: This is the answer to a team living on bubbles and quick outs.

coaching.install: Three interior linemen covering both guards and the centre. Nobody inside gets a free release to the second level.
coaching.commentary: Built for a team that wants to run inside zone at you all afternoon.

coaching.keys: Six rushers against five blockers. One of them comes free and the ball has to be out before he arrives.
coaching.commentary: The quarterback's hot answer has to be built in, because the protection cannot hold this.

coaching.install: Four down, four linebackers, three deep. Every gap has a defender before the ball is snapped.
coaching.commentary: Common at the youth and small-school level for a reason: it stops the run without asking anybody to think.

coaching.keys: Outside linebackers carry the backs. Everything else is man with a free safety in the middle.
Both outside linebackers come off the edge and squeeze everything back inside to the pursuit.
coaching.commentary: Vulnerable to anything that gets outside them, which is why it is a down-and-distance call.

coaching.keys: Trail technique underneath with two safeties over the top. Nothing goes over anybody's head.
coaching.commentary: Concedes the check-down and takes away everything past ten yards.

coaching.keys: The Mike runs the deep middle to twenty. The two safeties play true halves behind him.

coaching.install: Two defenders on their best receiver, one under and one over. Everyone else is on an island.
coaching.commentary: The call for a team with one player who beats you and four who do not.

coaching.keys: Both ends rush from outside the tight end, so the quarterback's edge disappears before his third step.
coaching.commentary: Wide alignment gives up the inside run, which is the trade you accept on an obvious passing down.

coaching.keys: The robber sits at ten in the middle of the field and takes the first crosser he sees.

coaching.install: Both linebackers mug the A gaps and cross on the snap, so the centre has to pick one and guess.
coaching.keys: The second rusher through is the one who gets home.

coaching.commentary: Six rushers with no safety help. It ends the drive or it ends the game.

coaching.keys: The corner comes off the boundary edge and the safety rotates over the top to replace him.
coaching.commentary: Time it to a formation into the boundary and the back has nobody to pick up.

coaching.install: Five rush, three under, three deep. The end who drops is the one the protection counted on rushing.
coaching.keys: Pressure from the backside meets a quarterback who is looking the other way.

coaching.install: Show two high, roll late. The strong safety buzzes to a hook and the free safety takes the middle third.
coaching.commentary: The picture the quarterback saw pre-snap is gone by the time he finishes his drop.

coaching.keys: Three down linemen two-gap while the corners trap anything that shows in the flat.

coaching.commentary: Built for spread teams: five defensive backs, a robber in the middle, and enough bodies to still fit the run.

coaching.keys: Corners trap number two in the flat. Safeties take number one whenever that happens.
The corner squats on the flat and the safety takes his third.

coaching.commentary: Seven-on-seven is where one receiver can decide a whole tournament. Put two on him.

coaching.install: Two deep halves and one underneath. Nothing gets over the top and everything short is open.
coaching.commentary: Call it when they only need a big play, which in flag is most of the fourth quarter.

coaching.keys: Line up on them at the line. With a seven-second clock, a route that starts late never gets thrown.
coaching.commentary: Check your league's contact rules before installing this one.

coaching.keys: Two rushers from seven yards leaves three defenders on three receivers with nobody deep.
coaching.commentary: A gamble that wins the down or gives up the game. Save it.

coaching.keys: The safety starts deep and comes late, so the quarterback never counts him as a rusher.
